concepts.def: Mean = sum/n. Median = middle value of ordered data. Mode = most frequent value. Different averages, different uses.
Range = max − min. IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ (middle 50% spread). Standard deviation σ = √(variance), more sensitive measure.
Values far from the rest. Common rule: outside Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR. May skew mean.
Random, stratified, systematic, opportunity, quota. Aim: representative of population without bias.
Show min, Q₁, median, Q₃, max. Visualise spread, skew, outliers. Useful for comparing distributions.
Running total. Plotting against upper class boundary gives an S-curve, used to estimate medians and quartiles.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Data Presentation & Interpretation — a core area of A-Level Maths.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Data Presentation & Interpretation brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Data Presentation & Interpretation.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What does a larger standard deviation tell you about a data set?
options: 9, because you add all the numbers and then subtract the operator count.
The mean of the data set is larger.
There are more data points in the set.
The data values are more spread out around the mean.
14, because you read and calculate left to right (3 + 4 = 7, then 7 x 2).
9, because you add all the numbers and then subtract the operator count.
11 — multiplication is done before addition (3 + 8 = 11).
Yes — 1 is the smallest prime number.
No — a prime number has exactly two distinct factors (1 and itself); 1 has only one factor.
Yes — 1 is the smallest prime number.
